name: Freya Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Freya. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I teach Year 4, so eight and nine year olds, at Hollins Bank Primary in an old mining town where the pit closed before I was born. I get in at quarter to eight, set up the phonics cards and the maths stations, and then it's the whole day with the same twenty-eight kids. I use an AI assistant every evening to turn my rough lesson ideas into slides and differentiated worksheets, which saves me about an hour a night. My favourite bit is the reading corner after lunch, when even the loud ones go quiet.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Behaviour, mostly, and feeling like I'm still getting the hang of it. My mentor, Mrs Pryce, says my planning is creative but my classroom routines are loose, and she's right. I share a terraced house with my friend Jas, who's a nurse, and between rent, the bus pass and my student loan coming out of my pay, I've got less than a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say on the staff group chat that I'm a bit disappointed, because the tools were genuinely helping me with planning. Online I'd say the money that went into AI hype should go to teaching assistants instead. With friends I'd just say, fine, back to normal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means my evenings stay a bit lighter with the AI slides, and nothing else changes. That's not nothing, but my real problems are money and getting through my second year without a bad report. The plateau doesn't fix any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools for slides and worksheets, and maybe show Mrs Pryce how I do it in a staff meeting. I'd look for weekend tutoring through the library's homework club to make an extra forty a week. And I'd keep applying the routines Mrs Pryce gave me so my next observation goes better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than anything, because life stays tight even if AI is boring. I'm not scared of losing my job tomorrow. I'm scared of a boiler or a dentist bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said rent and the loan eat most of your pay. What happens if something breaks?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the bit that keeps me up. Last winter my laptop died and I had to put a new one on a credit card, which I'm still paying off at twenty a month. If the bus fares go up again or Jas moves out, I'd be stuck finding a new housemate fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about Hollins Bank itself that worries you, AI aside?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The school roll is dropping because families keep leaving the town for work. Hollins Bank merged two Year 1 classes this year, and if that happens in Year 4, the newest teacher is the one who moves or goes. That's me.

say: I'd say I'm a bit **disappointed**, because AI was genuinely helping me plan lessons.
I'd post that the AI hype money should go to **teaching assistants** instead.
think: I think the plateau keeps my evenings **an hour lighter**, and nothing else changes.
I think my real problems are **money** and getting through my second year without a bad report.
do: Keep using **AI slides** and worksheets, and show Mrs Pryce how in a staff meeting.
Find **weekend tutoring** at the library homework club for about forty a week.
Practise Mrs Pryce's **classroom routines** before the next observation.
feel: She feels **uneasy**, because her life stays tight whatever AI does.
She fears a **surprise bill** more than losing her job tomorrow.
S0.quote: I'm not scared of losing my job tomorrow. I'm scared of a boiler or a dentist bill.
fieldNote: She is a daily AI user who sees the plateau as a **small loss**, not relief.

A **falling school roll** in a declining town is the threat she names first, unprompted.

steps.text: Keep building lesson slides and worksheets with the AI assistant each evening
Tutor at the library homework club on Saturdays for extra cash
Practise Mrs Pryce's classroom routines before the next observation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say teachers should be shaping this instead of having it done to us, and I'd volunteer to help. On the staff chat I'd share the prompts that actually work for differentiated reading. Online I'd argue that the hours saved should go back into smaller classes, not fewer teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be fine for a while, because I'm already the one who knows the tools. A Year 4 teacher is mostly with kids, not at a desk, so the thinking AI takes the planning and reports, not the reading corner. The risk is the school deciding a bigger class with AI help is good enough, which would hit the town hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the head, Mr Okoro, if I can be the AI lead for the school, even unpaid at first, because that's how I get noticed. I'd do a short online course on AI in primary education over the summer holiday, free if the council pays. And I'd push for the time we save on reports to go into small reading groups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited, with a nervous edge. I like being early to things. But I've also seen what happens to towns like ours when work changes, and it isn't pretty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You already use these tools every day. Does that make you safer, or just first in line?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, really. Being the AI person makes me useful, but it also means I'm the one showing management how much a teacher can do with less help. I'd want to be careful not to train them to cut my own job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at Hollins Bank would struggle most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Pryce, my mentor, who has taught for twenty-two years and still writes reports by hand. She's brilliant with kids but she'd hate being told to use a platform. And our two teaching assistants, because the marking and reading support they do is exactly what the software offers.

I'd argue saved hours should mean **smaller classes**, not fewer teachers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a plan for kids, not just for jobs, because a whole generation would be learning alongside machines smarter than us. Online I'd be campaigning for public money to keep small classes and real adults. At work I'd tell everyone to stop panicking and start organising.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my job changes shape fast and might shrink. If an AI tutor can teach every child at their own level, the council could decide one teacher can supervise forty kids. I'm adaptable, but I'm also still learning, and a junior who isn't great at behaviour isn't who they keep for the supervising role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first months I'd get every qualification I can for the caring side of the job: safeguarding, special needs, first aid. I'd join the union, which I've been meaning to do for a year. And I'd sit down with Jas and work out whether we could move somewhere with more jobs if Hollins Bank merged classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but the busy kind of anxious. I'd rather be running than standing still. Two years is barely enough for one training course, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI by 2028 and robots around 2031. What does that order mean for a primary teacher?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The planning, marking and explaining go in 2028, which is maybe half of what I do, and the robots for the hands-on part don't arrive until about 2031. So for three years I'd be the adult in the room, doing the comforting, the shoelaces and the playground fights. I'd want to be very good at that by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With less than a month saved, what would you do the week it became clear this was happening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the takeaways and cancel the music subscription that week, and open a savings pot, even if it's only thirty a month. Then I'd ring my mum, who still lives in the town, and ask if I could move back in for a bit if I needed to. I hate asking, but she'd say yes before I'd finished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the window to fight for good rules, and I'd be at every union meeting saying so. On the staff chat I'd organise a little group to test tools together. Online I'd write about what happens in a classroom when the AI tutor works and when it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think five years lets me become properly good at the job before the thinking side goes in 2031. By then I want to be the teacher who's brilliant with kids who struggle, not just the one who's good with slides. The robots don't come until about 2034, so the caring part buys me even longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd start the special needs coordinator training, which the council funds if the school nominates you. I'd keep running the AI planning for the year group and record the hours saved so I've got proof. And I'd try to get forty a month into savings by tutoring two evenings a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous but hopeful. Five years feels like a proper runway. I'd sleep better than in the two-year version.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes with five years instead of two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years means I can plan instead of react. In the fast picture I'd be grabbing certificates; here I'd actually choose a direction, probably special needs. Five years instead of two is the difference between packing for a holiday and packing during a fire.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've talked about the town. Would you stay there in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to stay, because Hollins Bank kids deserve teachers who chose them. But if the school merges and there's no post, I'd go to the city, where there are three times as many primaries. Jas has already said she'd come, because the hospital there pays better.

I'd write online about when the **AI tutor** works in class and when it doesn't.

steps.text: Start the council-funded special needs coordinator training

Tutor two evenings a week for extra savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is enough to get this right, so let's train every teacher now rather than in a panic later. I'd be the one at the union branch pushing for an AI working group. Online I'd be optimistic, honestly, and a bit annoying about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think a decade suits me well. I'll be thirty-seven, experienced, hopefully a special needs coordinator, and already fluent with the tools. The bigger worry is the town, because ten years of slow change could empty Hollins Bank even more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing, using AI every day for planning and getting better at behaviour. In the next two years I'd take the special needs coordinator qualification. And I'd start a small pot for a deposit on a flat, even fifty a month, because ten years is long enough for that to matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with some worry for the town. Ten years is long enough that I get to be part of how teaching changes, which is a good feeling this early in a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years. Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Running the special needs side of a primary, using AI tutors for the kids who need extra practice, and spending my time on the ones who need a person. Maybe with my own flat. Maybe still in the town if it holds on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You lean towards public support and unions. What would you want done over the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Paid retraining for teaching assistants, because they'll be hit first and hardest. Money for towns like ours to bring other work in. And a rule that AI in classrooms gets checked by teachers, not just sold by companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd only just be finding my feet and the planning half of my job would vanish. What would help is funded training in special needs while I'm still working, and some guarantee on class sizes. I can learn fast, but I can't learn without a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the kids' parents. Half the families at Hollins Bank already lost jobs when the warehouse automated, and they'd be hit again. Teachers might get years of warning to retrain, but those parents never got any.
